topic: Right ventricular infarction with nitrate-induced hypotension
vignette: A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 50 minutes after the onset of crushing substernal chest pressure that began while he was shoveling snow. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia and smokes 1 pack of cigarettes daily. Medications are lisinopril, metformin, and atorvastatin. Paramedics gave him 325 mg of chewable aspirin en route.

On arrival, temperature is 36.9 C (98.4 F), blood pressure is 122/78 mm Hg, pulse is 74/min, respirations are 18/min, and pulse oximetry shows 96% on room air. He is diaphoretic. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Heart sounds are regular with no murmurs. ECG shows 3-mm ST-segment elevations in leads II, III, and aVF, with greater elevation in lead III than in lead II; 1-mm ST-segment elevation in lead V1; and reciprocal ST-segment depressions in leads I and aVL. The cardiac catheterization laboratory is activated, and sublingual nitroglycerin is given for ongoing chest pain.

Eight minutes later, the patient says he feels lightheaded. Blood pressure is 78/48 mm Hg and pulse is 88/min. Jugular venous pressure is 12 cm H<sub>2</sub>O. The lungs remain clear, and the extremities are cool.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Dobutamine infusion

why_correct: This patient has an inferior STEMI (ST elevation in II, III, and aVF), usually caused by occlusion of the right coronary artery. Two ECG clues point to right ventricular (RV) involvement: ST elevation greater in lead III than in lead II, and ST elevation in V1. RV infarction accompanies roughly 30%–50% of inferior MIs.

An infarcted RV cannot generate much pressure, so it depends on high filling pressure (preload) to push blood through the lungs to the left ventricle. Nitroglycerin is a venodilator; it drops preload, and left ventricular filling and cardiac output collapse. The result is the classic triad of RV infarction: hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and clear lungs.

The fix is to restore preload: stop nitrates and give an IV isotonic crystalloid bolus while the patient goes for emergent PCI, which is the definitive therapy. Right-sided precordial leads (ST elevation ≥1 mm in V4R) confirm the diagnosis.

why_wrong.A: Dobutamine is the inotrope of choice for RV infarction, but only when hypotension persists after adequate volume loading. Fluids come first.
why_wrong.B: An IABP lowers left ventricular afterload and augments coronary diastolic perfusion; it does not fix an RV preload problem. The IABP-SHOCK II trial also showed no mortality benefit from routine IABP use in MI complicated by cardiogenic shock.
why_wrong.C: Furosemide reduces preload further and would worsen the hypotension. The lungs are clear, so there is no pulmonary edema to treat.
why_wrong.D: Beta-blockers are contraindicated in patients with hypotension, signs of a low-output state, or increased risk of cardiogenic shock. IV metoprolol here could precipitate shock.

objective: In inferior STEMI, hypotension after nitrates with elevated JVP and clear lungs means RV infarction. Treat with IV fluids and urgent reperfusion, and avoid preload-reducing drugs (nitrates, diuretics, morphine).
sources: O'Gara PT, et al. 2013 ACCF/AHA Guideline for the Management of ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction. Circulation. 2013;127:e362–e425 (RV infarction section).
Rao SV, et al. 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI Guideline for the Management of Patients With Acute Coronary Syndromes. Circulation. 2025.
Thiele H, et al. Intraaortic balloon support for myocardial infarction with cardiogenic shock (IABP-SHOCK II). N Engl J Med. 2012;367:1287–1296.

topic: Tubal ectopic pregnancy with a contraindication to methotrexate (breastfeeding)
vignette: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, comes to the emergency department because of 2 days of vaginal spotting and intermittent left lower abdominal cramping. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. She delivered her second child vaginally 10 months ago and continues to breastfeed several times daily. She was treated for chlamydial cervicitis 6 years ago. Her only medication is a prenatal vitamin.

Temperature is 36.8 C (98.2 F), blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg, pulse is 82/min, and respirations are 14/min. The abdomen is soft, with mild left lower quadrant tenderness and no rebound or guarding. Pelvic examination shows a small amount of dark blood in the vaginal vault, a closed cervical os, and mild left adnexal tenderness. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows no intrauterine gestational sac and a 2.4-cm left adnexal mass, separate from the ovary, that contains a yolk sac without embryonic cardiac activity. There is no free fluid in the pelvis.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Dilation and curettage

why_correct: An extrauterine gestational sac containing a yolk sac, with no intrauterine pregnancy, confirms a tubal ectopic pregnancy. She is hemodynamically stable, the mass is small (2.4 cm), β-hCG is below 5,000 mIU/mL, there is no cardiac activity, and there is no sign of rupture. On paper she is an ideal methotrexate candidate, except for one detail: she is breastfeeding.

ACOG lists current breastfeeding as an absolute contraindication to methotrexate, because the drug passes into breast milk and can harm the infant. A hemodynamically stable patient who cannot receive methotrexate is treated surgically, usually by laparoscopy with salpingectomy (removing the tube) or salpingostomy (removing the pregnancy and preserving the tube). Because she is Rh-positive, anti-D immune globulin is not needed.

Other absolute contraindications worth memorizing: intrauterine pregnancy, immunodeficiency, moderate to severe anemia, leukopenia, or thrombocytopenia, methotrexate sensitivity, active pulmonary disease, active peptic ulcer disease, clinically significant hepatic or renal dysfunction, and ruptured ectopic pregnancy or hemodynamic instability. Relative contraindications include embryonic cardiac activity, β-hCG above 5,000 mIU/mL, a large mass (often cited as greater than 3.5–4 cm), refusal of blood transfusion, and inability to follow up.

why_wrong.A: D&C helps distinguish a failed intrauterine pregnancy from an ectopic pregnancy when the pregnancy location is unknown. Here the ectopic pregnancy is already visualized, and D&C would not treat it.
why_wrong.B: She meets the size and β-hCG criteria, but breastfeeding is an absolute contraindication to methotrexate.
why_wrong.D: Mifepristone followed by misoprostol is used for medication abortion or early loss of an intrauterine pregnancy. It does not treat a tubal pregnancy and would delay definitive care.
why_wrong.E: Serial β-hCG measurement is used for a pregnancy of unknown location. Expectant management of a known ectopic pregnancy is reserved for asymptomatic patients with low and declining β-hCG; she is symptomatic, and the diagnosis is already established.

objective: Breastfeeding is an absolute contraindication to methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy. Stable patients who cannot receive methotrexate are managed with laparoscopic surgery.
sources: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 193: Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy. Obstet Gynecol. 2018;131(3):e91–e103.

topic: Diabetic ketoacidosis with hypokalemia: replete potassium before insulin
vignette: A 22-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department because of 2 days of nausea, vomiting, and diffuse abdominal pain. She ran out of insulin 4 days ago after losing her health insurance. She reports increased thirst and urination.

Temperature is 37.2 C (99 F), blood pressure is 98/62 mm Hg, pulse is 118/min, and respirations are 30/min and deep. She is drowsy but oriented. Mucous membranes are dry, and her breath has a fruity odor. The abdomen is diffusely tender without rebound or guarding. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with prominent U waves. An infusion of isotonic crystalloid is started at 1 L/h.
stem: In addition to continued intravenous fluids, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Addition of 5% dextrose to the intravenous fluids
options.C: Intravenous insulin infusion plus intravenous potassium chloride
options.D: Intravenous potassium chloride, with insulin withheld

why_correct: This is severe DKA: glucose 486 mg/dL, β-hydroxybutyrate 7.8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 7 mEq/L, and an anion gap of 29 (132 − [96 + 7]). She needs insulin, but not yet.

Insulin drives potassium into cells by stimulating Na+/K+-ATPase. Patients in DKA have a large total-body potassium deficit from osmotic diuresis, vomiting, and volume-driven aldosterone release. Insulin deficiency, hyperosmolality, and acidosis shift potassium out of cells, so the serum level is usually normal or high at presentation. A low serum potassium at presentation (2.9 mEq/L, with U waves) therefore signals a profound deficit, and starting insulin now could cause life-threatening hypokalemia, arrhythmias, and respiratory muscle weakness.

The 2024 ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus report recommends starting potassium replacement and postponing insulin until serum potassium is above 3.5 mEq/L. (The older 2009 statement used 3.3 mEq/L; at 2.9 mEq/L the answer is the same under either.) Once potassium is above 3.5, start the insulin infusion and add potassium to the fluids to keep it in the normal range.

why_wrong.A: Dextrose is added once glucose falls to roughly 200–250 mg/dL, so the insulin infusion can keep clearing ketones without causing hypoglycemia. At 486 mg/dL it is not yet needed.
why_wrong.B: Insulin alone would push potassium further into cells and could precipitate a fatal arrhythmia.
why_wrong.C: The most tempting distractor. Giving insulin together with potassium is correct when potassium is 3.5 mEq/L or higher, but below 3.5 the consensus recommends postponing insulin until potassium has been repleted.
why_wrong.E: The 2024 consensus recommends bicarbonate only if pH is below 7.0. Her pH is 7.06, and bicarbonate would also shift potassium into cells and worsen her hypokalemia.

objective: Always check potassium before starting insulin in DKA. If K<sup>+</sup> is below 3.5 mEq/L, replace potassium first and hold insulin until K<sup>+</sup> is above 3.5 mEq/L.
sources: Umpierrez GE, et al. Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report. Diabetes Care. 2024;47(8):1257–1275 (also published in Diabetologia. 2024;67:1455–1479).

topic: Neonatal bilious emesis: rule out malrotation with midgut volvulus
vignette: A 3-day-old boy in the newborn nursery has had 3 episodes of forceful, bright green emesis over the past 3 hours. He was born at 39 weeks' gestation by uncomplicated vaginal delivery to a 28-year-old woman whose prenatal course, including fetal ultrasonography, was normal. Birth weight was 3.4 kg (7.5 lb). He passed meconium within 24 hours of birth and had been breastfeeding well.

Temperature is 37.0 C (98.6 F), pulse is 158/min, respirations are 44/min, and blood pressure is 72/46 mm Hg. He is alert and cries vigorously. The abdomen is soft and nondistended, with no tenderness or masses. The anus is normally positioned, and there is yellow stool in the diaper. A nasogastric tube is placed and returns bilious fluid. Abdominal x-ray shows a normal bowel gas pattern with gas in the rectum, no dilated loops, and no free air.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Abdominal ultrasonography of the pylorus

why_correct: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is a surgical emergency, and malrotation with midgut volvulus must be ruled out first. Volvulus can strangle the superior mesenteric artery and cause necrosis of the entire midgut within hours.

The trap is the reassuring picture: a vigorous infant, a soft abdomen, stool in the diaper, and a normal x-ray. Early volvulus often looks exactly like this, because the obstruction is proximal and the distal bowel has not yet emptied. A normal x-ray does not rule it out.

In a hemodynamically stable infant, the upper GI contrast series is the diagnostic study of choice. It shows an abnormally positioned duodenojejunal junction (malrotation) or a “corkscrew” duodenum (volvulus). While it is arranged, the infant is kept NPO with nasogastric decompression and IV fluids, and pediatric surgery is consulted. Infants with peritonitis or shock skip imaging and go straight to laparotomy (Ladd procedure).
Pearl: duodenal atresia also causes bilious vomiting, usually on day 1, but its x-ray shows a “double bubble” with no distal gas. This infant has rectal gas.

why_wrong.A: Pyloric stenosis presents at about 3–6 weeks of age with nonbilious projectile vomiting, because the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla of Vater.
why_wrong.B: A contrast enema evaluates distal obstruction (Hirschsprung disease, meconium plug, meconium ileus), which presents with failure to pass meconium and abdominal distension. This infant passed meconium and is not distended.
why_wrong.C: Rectal suction biopsy diagnoses Hirschsprung disease (absent ganglion cells), which classically presents with delayed passage of meconium beyond 48 hours and distension.
why_wrong.D: Bilious emesis is never normal in a newborn. Reassurance risks missing a volvulus until the bowel is dead.

objective: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise. Stable infants get an emergent upper GI series; unstable infants or those with peritonitis go directly to surgery.
sources: American College of Radiology. ACR Appropriateness Criteria: Vomiting in Infants.
Sizemore AW, et al. Diagnostic performance of the upper GI series in children with suspected malrotation. Pediatr Radiol (UGI sensitivity about 96% for surgically confirmed malrotation).

topic: Acetaminophen overdose with unknown ingestion time
vignette: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her roommate, who returned from a weekend away and found her in her bedroom with an empty bottle of extra-strength acetaminophen (500-mg tablets) and a note apologizing to her family. The patient says she took “a lot of pills” but is unsure when; she thinks it was “sometime yesterday or the day before.” She reports nausea and right upper abdominal discomfort. She takes no other medications and denies other ingestions.

Temperature is 37.0 C (98.6 F), blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg, pulse is 96/min, and respirations are 16/min. She is alert, oriented, and tearful. There is mild right upper quadrant tenderness. There is no jaundice or asterixis.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Activated charcoal
options.E: Repeat acetaminophen level in 4 hours and plot on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram

why_correct: The Rumack-Matthew nomogram works only for a single acute ingestion with a known time of ingestion, using a level drawn 4–24 hours afterward. This patient cannot say when she took the pills, so the nomogram cannot be used. She also already has a detectable acetaminophen level and elevated aminotransferases, meaning liver injury is underway.

The 2023 US/Canadian consensus statement recommends starting N-acetylcysteine (NAC) immediately when the time of ingestion is unknown and the acetaminophen concentration is detectable or aminotransferases are elevated. NAC replenishes glutathione, which detoxifies the toxic metabolite NAPQI. It is most protective within 8 hours of ingestion, but it still improves outcomes when started late, including after liver injury has begun. Treatment continues until acetaminophen is undetectable and liver tests and INR are improving.
Because this was an intentional overdose with a suicide note, she also needs continuous observation and psychiatric evaluation once she is medically stable.

why_wrong.A: Activated charcoal helps when given within about 4 hours of ingestion. Her ingestion was likely more than a day ago, so charcoal offers no benefit and adds aspiration risk.
why_wrong.B: Extracorporeal removal is reserved for massive ingestions with extremely high acetaminophen concentrations plus altered mental status and metabolic acidosis. She has a modest level, normal mentation, and normal pH and lactate.
why_wrong.D: She does not meet King's College criteria for transplant referral in acetaminophen-induced liver failure: arterial pH below 7.30 after resuscitation, or all of INR above 6.5, creatinine above 3.4 mg/dL, and grade III or IV encephalopathy.
why_wrong.E: Waiting 4 hours delays the antidote while liver injury progresses, and a second level still cannot be plotted without a known ingestion time.

objective: The Rumack-Matthew nomogram applies only to a single acute ingestion with a known time. If the time is unknown and acetaminophen is detectable or AST/ALT is elevated, start NAC immediately.
sources: Dart RC, et al. Management of Acetaminophen Poisoning in the US and Canada: A Consensus Statement. JAMA Netw Open. 2023;6(8):e2327739.
O'Grady JG, et al. Early indicators of prognosis in fulminant hepatic failure. Gastroenterology. 1989;97:439–445 (King's College criteria).

topic: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with thrombosis
vignette: A 72-year-old woman is hospitalized for community-acquired pneumonia. On admission, she was started on ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and subcutaneous unfractionated heparin 5,000 units every 8 hours for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Her fever and oxygen requirement have improved. On hospital day 7, she reports new pain and swelling in her right calf.

Vital signs are within normal limits. The right calf is 3 cm larger in circumference than the left and is tender. There is no bleeding from any site. Duplex ultrasonography shows an occlusive thrombus in the right popliteal vein. A peripheral blood smear shows no schistocytes. A platelet factor 4 (PF4)–heparin immunoassay is sent.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Discontinue heparin and await immunoassay results

why_correct: This is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT): IgG antibodies against PF4–heparin complexes activate platelets, causing thrombocytopenia and a strongly prothrombotic state. Her 4Ts score is high: platelets fell 63% with a nadir above 20,000/µL (2 points), the fall began on day 7 of heparin (2 points), and she has a new DVT (2 points). The antibiotics are a possible alternative cause (1 point), for a total of 7 of 8.

With an intermediate or high 4Ts score, ASH recommends stopping all heparin (including flushes) and immediately starting a non-heparin anticoagulant at therapeutic intensity, without waiting for lab confirmation. Options include argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, or a DOAC. Argatroban is hepatically cleared, which makes it a good choice here and in renal failure. Because she has HIT with thrombosis, therapeutic dosing is required.

why_wrong.A: Stopping heparin without starting another anticoagulant leaves her at high risk of new thrombosis, and she already has a DVT that needs treatment. The immunoassay guides later decisions; it does not delay treatment when the 4Ts score is high.
why_wrong.C: Low-molecular-weight heparin cross-reacts with HIT antibodies, so enoxaparin is contraindicated in acute HIT.
why_wrong.D: Starting warfarin during acute HIT rapidly depletes protein C and can cause venous limb gangrene. ASH recommends against starting warfarin before platelet recovery (at least 150,000/µL) and favors transitioning to a DOAC rather than warfarin.
why_wrong.E: HIT is a clotting disorder, and bleeding is uncommon. Platelet transfusion is generally avoided unless there is active bleeding or a high-bleeding-risk procedure.

objective: With an intermediate or high 4Ts score, stop all heparin and immediately start a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, or a DOAC). Avoid LMWH, avoid warfarin until platelets recover, and avoid prophylactic platelet transfusion.
sources: Cuker A, et al. American Society of Hematology 2018 guidelines for management of venous thromboembolism: heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Blood Adv. 2018;2(22):3360–3392.

topic: Bacterial meningitis needing CT before LP: treat before imaging; add ampicillin after age 50
vignette: A 61-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband because of fever, severe headache, and increasing confusion that began 18 hours ago. She had right ear pain for several days last week. While in triage, she has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure that stops spontaneously after 2 minutes. Her only medical condition is hypothyroidism, treated with levothyroxine.

Temperature is 39.6 C (103.3 F), blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg, pulse is 116/min, respirations are 22/min, and pulse oximetry shows 95% on room air. She is postictal; she opens her eyes to voice but does not consistently follow commands. Passive neck flexion is resisted and painful. The right tympanic membrane is erythematous and bulging. There is no rash. She moves all extremities.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Blood cultures, then IV dexamethasone, vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and ampicillin, then CT of the head
options.B: Blood cultures, then IV vancomycin and ceftriaxone, then CT of the head
options.C: CT of the head, then lumbar puncture, then antibiotics based on CSF findings
options.D: Immediate lumbar puncture, then empiric antibiotics
options.E: Intravenous acyclovir, then MRI of the brain

why_correct: Fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status after a recent otitis media point to acute bacterial meningitis, most likely Streptococcus pneumoniae spreading from the middle ear.

She needs a head CT before lumbar puncture because she had a new-onset seizure and has an abnormal level of consciousness. (IDSA criteria for CT before LP: immunocompromise, history of CNS disease, new-onset seizure, papilledema, abnormal level of consciousness, or focal neurologic deficit.) But imaging must never delay treatment: draw blood cultures, give dexamethasone and empiric antibiotics, then obtain the CT, then perform the LP if it is safe.

Empiric therapy for adults older than 50 is vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime), plus ampicillin for Listeria monocytogenes. Dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours for 2–4 days) reduces unfavorable outcomes and death in adults with pneumococcal meningitis and should be given 10–20 minutes before, or together with, the first antibiotic dose.

why_wrong.B: Close, but it misses two things. Without ampicillin, Listeria (a major pathogen after age 50) is uncovered. And dexamethasone must be given with or before the first antibiotic dose; IDSA advises against starting it in adults who have already received antibiotics.
why_wrong.C: CT before LP is the right order, but antibiotics must not wait for either. Delaying antibiotics in bacterial meningitis increases mortality.
why_wrong.D: A new seizure and depressed consciousness raise concern for elevated intracranial pressure or a mass lesion (such as a brain abscess from otitis), so LP before CT risks herniation. It also delays antibiotics.
why_wrong.E: Acyclovir can be added when HSV encephalitis is a concern, but acyclovir alone leaves bacterial meningitis untreated, and MRI would delay care.

objective: In suspected bacterial meningitis with an indication for CT before LP, the order is blood cultures, then dexamethasone plus empiric antibiotics, then CT, then LP. After age 50, add ampicillin for Listeria.
sources: Tunkel AR, et al. Practice Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis. Clin Infect Dis. 2004;39(9):1267–1284.
de Gans J, van de Beek D. Dexamethasone in adults with bacterial meningitis. N Engl J Med. 2002;347:1549–1556.

topic: Hyponatremia overcorrection in a patient at high risk for osmotic demyelination
vignette: A 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his sister because of 3 days of progressive confusion, unsteady gait, and generalized weakness. He has alcohol use disorder and has been drinking about 18 cans of beer daily for the past 2 weeks while eating very little. He has no other medical conditions and takes no medications.

Temperature is 36.7 C (98.1 F), blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg, pulse is 92/min, and respirations are 16/min. He is thin and oriented to person only. Mucous membranes are moist, and there is no edema or asterixis. Neurologic examination is nonfocal, and there is no seizure activity. Admission laboratory results are as follows:
after_labs: He is admitted to the intensive care unit and treated with intravenous thiamine, potassium chloride (80 mEq over 8 hours), and 0.9% saline. Over the next 8 hours, he produces 3.6 L of dilute urine. Repeat serum sodium is 117 mEq/L. He is now oriented to person and place.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: 3% hypertonic saline
options.B: Continue current therapy and recheck sodium in 4 hours
options.D: Intravenous desmopressin and 5% dextrose in water

why_correct: This is beer potomania (low-solute hyponatremia). The kidneys need solute to excrete water. With almost no food and only beer, his solute intake is so low that he cannot excrete the water he drinks, even though ADH is appropriately suppressed (urine osmolality 70 mOsm/kg).

Once solute arrives (saline, potassium, and soon food), the kidneys suddenly excrete large volumes of dilute urine, and serum sodium rises fast and unpredictably. Potassium repletion raises serum sodium too, because exchangeable potassium counts toward serum sodium concentration. His sodium has already risen 10 mEq/L in 8 hours, and the water diuresis is ongoing.

He is at high risk for osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS): alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hypokalemia, and a starting sodium near 105. In high-risk patients the goal is a rise of 4–6 mEq/L per day, and the rise should not exceed 8 mEq/L in any 24-hour period. He has already passed that limit, so the next step is therapeutic relowering: desmopressin to stop the free-water loss plus electrolyte-free water (D5W) to bring sodium back below the limit.
Do not be reassured by his improved mental status. ODS symptoms (dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis, “locked-in” syndrome) typically appear 2–6 days after overly rapid correction.

why_wrong.A: Hypertonic saline is for severe symptoms (seizures, coma, respiratory distress) or acute hyponatremia. He is improving and has already corrected too fast.
why_wrong.B: With an ongoing water diuresis, sodium will keep climbing; rechecking in 4 hours just documents a larger overcorrection. Continuing saline adds more solute.
why_wrong.C: Fluid restriction is part of long-term management, but right now it would accelerate the rise in sodium.
why_wrong.E: Tolvaptan is a vasopressin V<sub>2</sub> receptor antagonist that increases free-water excretion, the opposite of what is needed. It would raise sodium even faster.

objective: In patients at high risk for ODS (alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hypokalemia, liver disease, sodium ≤105 mEq/L), do not exceed a sodium rise of 8 mEq/L in 24 hours. If a sudden water diuresis overshoots the limit, relower sodium with desmopressin plus D5W.
sources: Verbalis JG, et al. Diagnosis, evaluation, and treatment of hyponatremia: expert panel recommendations. Am J Med. 2013;126(10 Suppl 1):S1–S42.
Spasovski G, et al. Clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia. Eur J Endocrinol. 2014;170(3):G1–G47.
Rondon-Berrios H, et al. Review of therapeutic plasma sodium relowering after overly rapid correction of hyponatremia. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2020.

topic: Refeeding syndrome during treatment of anorexia nervosa
vignette: A 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa is admitted for nutritional rehabilitation after losing 14 kg (31 lb) over 6 months. Her body mass index is 14.1 kg/m<sup>2</sup>. On admission, blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg, pulse is 46/min, and temperature is 35.8 C (96.4 F). She receives oral thiamine and a multivitamin, and a meal-based refeeding plan is started with daily increases in calories. Admission laboratory results are listed below.

On hospital day 3, she develops swelling of both legs, generalized weakness, and confusion. Pulse is 118/min and respirations are 24/min. Crackles are heard at both lung bases. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a corrected QT interval of 510 msec.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Administer intravenous furosemide for the edema
options.B: Begin intravenous phosphate, potassium, and magnesium replacement and slow the caloric advancement
options.C: Increase caloric intake to correct her malnutrition faster
options.D: Start a continuous insulin infusion for hyperglycemia

why_correct: This is refeeding syndrome. After prolonged starvation, reintroducing carbohydrate triggers insulin release, which drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells and consumes thiamine. The result is hypophosphatemia (ATP depletion: weakness, confusion, respiratory and cardiac dysfunction), hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia (arrhythmia, QT prolongation), and insulin-driven sodium and water retention (edema).

The 2020 ASPEN consensus defines refeeding syndrome as a fall in phosphorus, potassium, or magnesium within 5 days of restarting calories, graded mild (10%–20% drop), moderate (20%–30%), or severe (more than 30% or organ dysfunction). Her phosphorus fell 66% and she has edema, confusion, and a prolonged QT: this is severe.

Treatment is to replace the electrolytes intravenously with cardiac monitoring, continue thiamine (typically 100 mg daily before and during the first days of refeeding), and slow or temporarily reduce the caloric advancement until the electrolytes are stable, then resume with daily monitoring. Nutrition is not stopped altogether; the goal is a controlled pace.

why_wrong.A: The edema comes from insulin-mediated sodium retention, and she is already hypovolemic and bradycardic. Furosemide would worsen her hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia.
why_wrong.C: Pushing calories faster accelerates the intracellular shifts that are causing the problem. This is the most dangerous choice.
why_wrong.D: Insulin would drive even more phosphate and potassium into cells. Mild refeeding hyperglycemia is treated by slowing carbohydrate delivery, not with an insulin drip.
why_wrong.E: The route is not the problem, and parenteral nutrition carries a higher refeeding risk than enteral or oral feeding.

objective: Falling phosphorus, potassium, or magnesium within 5 days of restarting nutrition in a malnourished patient is refeeding syndrome. Replace electrolytes, give thiamine, and slow the caloric advancement; never speed it up.
sources: da Silva JSV, et al. ASPEN Consensus Recommendations for Refeeding Syndrome. Nutr Clin Pract. 2020;35(2):178–195.

topic: Sigmoid volvulus after successful endoscopic detorsion: resect during the same admission
vignette: An 81-year-old man is brought from his nursing facility because of 2 days of abdominal distension, crampy pain, and no passage of stool or flatus. He has Parkinson disease and chronic constipation. Temperature is 37.1 C (98.8 F), blood pressure is 134/78 mm Hg, and pulse is 92/min. The abdomen is markedly distended and tympanitic, with mild diffuse tenderness and no rebound or guarding. Leukocyte count is 9,800/µL and serum lactate is 1.4 mmol/L. Abdominal x-ray shows a massively dilated, ahaustral loop of colon arising from the pelvis and extending to the right upper quadrant. CT shows a swirl of mesenteric vessels at the sigmoid colon, normal bowel wall enhancement, and no free air.

He undergoes flexible sigmoidoscopy with successful detorsion and decompression; the mucosa appears viable, and a rectal tube is left in place. Over the next 48 hours he passes flatus and stool, the abdomen becomes soft and nondistended, and he tolerates a regular diet. The anesthesiologist considers him an acceptable, though higher-risk, operative candidate.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Discharge to the nursing facility with outpatient colonoscopy in 6 weeks
options.E: Sigmoidopexy (surgical fixation of the sigmoid colon without resection)

why_correct: A redundant sigmoid colon on a long, narrow mesentery twists on itself, producing a closed-loop obstruction. The classic patient is elderly, institutionalized, chronically constipated, and often on medications that slow the bowel. The x-ray shows the coffee-bean sign, and the CT shows the mesenteric whirl sign.

In a stable patient without peritonitis or perforation, the first step is endoscopic detorsion and decompression, which also lets the endoscopist inspect the mucosa for ischemia. That was done correctly here. The trap is to stop there: recurrence after detorsion alone is very high (commonly cited at 40%–60% or more), and each recurrence carries more risk of necrosis and death.

The 2021 ASCRS guideline recommends that patients who undergo successful endoscopic detorsion be considered for sigmoid colectomy during the same hospital admission to prevent recurrence. Resection with primary anastomosis is usual in a prepared, stable patient; nonresectional operations are inferior. Urgent resection without a prior endoscopic attempt is reserved for failed detorsion, nonviable bowel, or perforation.

why_wrong.A: Discharge after detorsion alone invites recurrence, often within days to weeks, in a frail patient who tolerated one episode. Colonoscopy in 6 weeks does nothing to prevent the next twist.
why_wrong.B: Percutaneous endoscopic colostomy (endoscopic fixation) is an option only for patients whose operative risk is prohibitive. He is an acceptable candidate.
why_wrong.C: Repeating the sigmoidoscopy adds information only if there is concern for ischemia; it does not treat the underlying redundant sigmoid.
why_wrong.E: Sigmoidopexy, detorsion alone, and mesosigmoidoplasty all have higher recurrence rates than resection, so the guideline recommends colectomy instead.

objective: Sigmoid volvulus in a stable patient: endoscopic detorsion first, then sigmoid colectomy during the same admission. Cecal volvulus skips endoscopy and goes straight to right colectomy.
sources: Alavi K, et al. The American Society of Colon and Rectal Surgeons Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Colonic Volvulus and Acute Colonic Pseudo-Obstruction. Dis Colon Rectum. 2021;64(9):1046–1057.

topic: Complicated parapneumonic effusion: drain it
vignette: A 58-year-old man with alcohol use disorder was admitted 3 days ago with right lower lobe community-acquired pneumonia and has been receiving intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin. After initial improvement, he now has recurrent fever to 39.0 C (102.2 F), right-sided pleuritic chest pain, and worsening dyspnea. Pulse is 104/min, respirations are 24/min, and pulse oximetry shows 92% on room air. Breath sounds are decreased at the right base with dullness to percussion.

Chest x-ray shows a right pleural effusion occupying about 40% of the hemithorax that layers freely on a lateral decubitus film. Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis yields cloudy yellow fluid without frank pus.
stem: In addition to continuing antibiotics, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Continue current antibiotics and repeat thoracentesis in 48 hours

why_correct: The fluid is an exudate by Light's criteria (pleural-to-serum protein ratio 0.72, LDH ratio 8.9, and LDH far above two-thirds of the upper limit of normal). More importantly, it is a complicated parapneumonic effusion: pleural fluid pH below 7.20, glucose below 60 mg/dL, and a very high LDH mean bacteria have invaded the pleural space, even though the Gram stain is negative and the fluid is not yet frank pus.

Pleural fluid pH, measured on a blood-gas analyzer, is the single most useful chemistry. A pH below 7.20 (or glucose below 60 mg/dL), a positive Gram stain or culture, a large effusion (at least half the hemithorax), or loculations place the patient in the ACCP moderate- or high-risk categories, where antibiotics alone fail and drainage is required. Untreated, the effusion organizes into empyema and a fibrous peel.

Drainage means a chest tube, ideally a small-bore tube placed under ultrasound guidance. Antibiotics should also cover anaerobes (for example, adding metronidazole or switching to ampicillin-sulbactam). If the fluid is loculated or drainage is incomplete, intrapleural tPA plus DNase (MIST2) or thoracoscopic drainage is the next escalation.

why_wrong.A: Waiting lets the fibrinopurulent stage progress to loculation and empyema. The decision to drain is already made by the fluid chemistry.
why_wrong.B: Corticosteroids have no role in treating an infected pleural space and may impair host defenses.
why_wrong.C: Intermittent taps rarely achieve complete drainage of an infected space; a tube provides continuous drainage and a route for fibrinolytics if needed.
why_wrong.D: Surgery is reserved for effusions that fail tube drainage with or without fibrinolytics, or for organized empyema. It is not the first step for a free-flowing effusion.

objective: A parapneumonic effusion with pH below 7.20, glucose below 60 mg/dL, positive Gram stain or culture, loculations, or frank pus needs tube drainage plus antibiotics with anaerobic coverage.
sources: Colice GL, et al. Medical and surgical treatment of parapneumonic effusions: an evidence-based guideline (ACCP). Chest. 2000;118(4):1158–1171.
Roberts ME, et al. British Thoracic Society Guideline for pleural disease. Thorax. 2023;78(Suppl 3).
Rahman NM, et al. Intrapleural use of tissue plasminogen activator and DNase in pleural infection (MIST2). N Engl J Med. 2011;365:518–526.

topic: Septic arthritis of the hip in a child (Kocher criteria)
vignette: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because he has refused to walk since waking this morning. He had a runny nose and cough last week that resolved. Temperature is 38.9 C (102 F) and pulse is 128/min. He lies with the right hip flexed, abducted, and externally rotated and cries with any passive motion of the hip. There is no rash or skin lesion. Radiographs of the pelvis and right hip are normal. Hip ultrasonography shows a moderate right hip effusion.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Arthrocentesis of the right hip under ultrasound guidance
options.B: Empiric intravenous cefazolin and reassessment in 24 hours
options.C: Ibuprofen and observation with repeat examination in 24 hours
options.E: Trial of weight bearing after acetaminophen

why_correct: The question is septic arthritis versus transient synovitis, and the Kocher criteria settle it: inability to bear weight, fever above 38.5 C, ESR above 40 mm/h, and leukocyte count above 12,000/µL. He has all four, which predicts septic arthritis in about 99% of cases (three of four predicts about 93%). An elevated CRP (above 2 mg/dL) adds further weight. The preceding viral illness is a red herring that would fit transient synovitis only if he were well-appearing with normal labs.

Septic arthritis of the hip is an emergency: bacterial enzymes destroy cartilage within days, and pressure in the capsule can cause avascular necrosis of the femoral head. The next step is joint aspiration, which confirms the diagnosis (synovial leukocytes typically above 50,000/µL with neutrophil predominance, Gram stain, culture) and should be obtained before antibiotics whenever possible so cultures are not sterilized.
Aspiration is followed promptly by intravenous antibiotics (covering Staphylococcus aureus and, in children under about 4 years, Kingella kingae) and surgical irrigation and drainage of the hip.

why_wrong.B: Antibiotics before aspiration lower the culture yield and, more importantly, delay the drainage the joint needs.
why_wrong.C: NSAIDs and observation are appropriate for transient synovitis, the diagnosis in a well-appearing, afebrile child with few or no Kocher criteria. Not here.
why_wrong.D: MRI helps when adjacent osteomyelitis or an abscess is suspected, but it should never delay aspiration of a joint with this probability of infection.
why_wrong.E: A child who meets all four criteria needs the joint drained, not a walking trial.

objective: In a child with an irritable hip, count the Kocher criteria (non-weight-bearing, fever above 38.5 C, ESR above 40, WBC above 12,000). Three or four mean septic arthritis until proven otherwise: aspirate the joint, then antibiotics and surgical drainage.
sources: Kocher MS, Zurakowski D, Kasser JR. Differentiating between septic arthritis and transient synovitis of the hip in children: an evidence-based clinical prediction algorithm. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1999;81(12):1662–1670.
Caird MS, et al. Factors distinguishing septic arthritis from transient synovitis of the hip in children. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2006;88(6):1251–1257.

topic: Suspected melanoma: narrow excisional biopsy first
vignette: A 46-year-old man comes to the office because his wife noticed that a mole on his upper back has grown and darkened over the past 6 months. He has fair skin, had several blistering sunburns as a child, and has no family history of skin cancer. Examination shows a 9-mm asymmetric, slightly raised lesion with irregular, notched borders and variegated brown and black color with a focal blue-gray area. Dermoscopy shows an atypical pigment network with a blue-white veil. There is no palpable cervical, axillary, or inguinal lymphadenopathy.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Excisional biopsy with 1- to 3-mm margins
options.B: Punch biopsy of the darkest area
options.C: Reassurance with photographic follow-up in 3 months

why_correct: The lesion has every ABCDE feature of melanoma (asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter above 6 mm, evolution), plus a blue-white veil on dermoscopy. The next step is histologic diagnosis with a technique that captures the whole lesion at full depth.

The American Academy of Dermatology recommends a narrow excisional (complete) biopsy with 1- to 3-mm margins, deep enough to avoid transecting the base. This provides the Breslow thickness, the single most important prognostic factor, along with ulceration and mitotic rate, which together determine the definitive excision margins and whether sentinel lymph node biopsy is offered.

Definitive treatment comes second: wide excision margins depend on Breslow depth (0.5–1 cm for melanoma in situ, 1 cm for tumors 1 mm or thinner, 1–2 cm for 1 to 2 mm, 2 cm for thicker than 2 mm). Sentinel lymph node biopsy is discussed for tumors 0.8 mm or thicker or any ulcerated tumor, and it is performed before or in the same operation as the wide excision.

why_wrong.B: A punch samples one part of a 9-mm lesion and can miss the thickest area, understaging the tumor. Partial biopsies are acceptable only for very large lesions or special sites when complete excision is impractical.
why_wrong.C: Delay in a lesion with this many melanoma features is never appropriate.
why_wrong.D: A superficial shave can transect the base of an invasive melanoma, making the Breslow thickness unmeasurable and compromising staging.
why_wrong.E: Margins cannot be chosen before the thickness is known, and a wide excision disturbs lymphatic drainage, which can make later sentinel node mapping unreliable.

objective: For a lesion suspicious for melanoma, do a narrow excisional biopsy with 1- to 3-mm margins first. Breslow thickness from that specimen dictates the wide excision margins and the need for sentinel lymph node biopsy.
sources: Swetter SM, et al. Guidelines of care for the management of primary cutaneous melanoma. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2019;80(1):208–250.

topic: Solid testicular mass: radical inguinal orchiectomy
vignette: A 26-year-old man comes to the office because of 2 months of painless enlargement of the left testis with an occasional dull ache. He underwent right orchiopexy for an undescended testis at age 2. Examination shows a 3-cm firm, nontender mass within the left testis that does not transilluminate. The right testis is normal. There is no gynecomastia or lymphadenopathy. Scrotal ultrasonography shows a 2.8-cm hypoechoic, heterogeneous, vascular solid mass within the left testis; the right testis is normal.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: CT-guided biopsy of retroperitoneal lymph nodes
options.E: Transscrotal needle biopsy of the mass

why_correct: A solid intratesticular mass is a malignant germ cell tumor until proven otherwise. He also has a classic risk factor: cryptorchidism (even after orchiopexy, and the risk applies to both testes). The AUA guideline is explicit: measure serum tumor markers (AFP, hCG, and LDH) before any treatment, then perform a radical inguinal orchiectomy, which is both the diagnostic biopsy and the definitive treatment of the primary tumor.

The inguinal approach ligates the spermatic cord at the internal ring and preserves the normal lymphatic anatomy: the testis drains to the para-aortic (retroperitoneal) nodes, while the scrotal skin drains to the inguinal nodes. Violating the scrotum can seed a second lymphatic pathway and upstage the disease.

Markers help with diagnosis and staging: AFP points to a nonseminomatous component (seminoma never raises AFP); hCG can be elevated in either. After orchiectomy, markers are repeated to their nadir and CT of the abdomen and pelvis (and chest imaging) stages the retroperitoneum. Sperm banking and a prosthesis are discussed before surgery.

why_wrong.A: Staging of the retroperitoneum is done with CT after orchiectomy, not by needle biopsy before the primary tumor has been removed.
why_wrong.C: Repeat imaging in 6 to 8 weeks is reserved for indeterminate findings with normal markers. A vascular solid mass with an elevated hCG is not indeterminate.
why_wrong.D: Testis-sparing surgery is not recommended when the contralateral testis is normal; it is considered only for bilateral tumors or a solitary testis.
why_wrong.E: Transscrotal biopsy is contraindicated because it breaches the scrotal lymphatics, risking local recurrence and inguinal spread.

objective: A solid testicular mass gets tumor markers (AFP, hCG, LDH) and then radical inguinal orchiectomy. Never biopsy or operate through the scrotum.
sources: Stephenson A, et al. Diagnosis and Treatment of Early-Stage Testicular Cancer: AUA Guideline. J Urol. 2019;202(2):272–281 (amended 2023).

topic: Confidential STI care for a minor
vignette: A 16-year-old girl comes alone to a community clinic because her 17-year-old boyfriend was diagnosed with chlamydia yesterday. She asks that her parents not be told; she is afraid they would make her leave home. She has no symptoms. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago, and a urine pregnancy test is negative. She is doing well in school, describes the relationship as consensual, and denies coercion, substance use, or concerns about her safety at home. A urine nucleic acid amplification test for Chlamydia trachomatis returns positive later that day; the test for Neisseria gonorrhoeae is negative.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Contact her parents to obtain consent before prescribing treatment
options.B: Refer her to a pediatrician who can obtain parental consent
options.C: Report the case to child protective services
options.D: Treat only after she agrees to inform her parents
options.E: Treat with doxycycline, counsel about confidentiality and partner treatment, and encourage her to talk with a trusted adult

why_correct: Every US state and the District of Columbia allow minors to consent to their own testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without parental involvement (a few states set a minimum age, typically 12 to 14). Confidential care is the standard endorsed by the AAP and the Society for Adolescent Health and Medicine, because fear of disclosure is a leading reason adolescents avoid care.

So the physician treats her and keeps the visit confidential. CDC-recommended treatment for uncomplicated chlamydia is doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days; azithromycin 1 g once is an alternative when adherence is a concern or in pregnancy. She should abstain from sex for 7 days after she and her partner complete treatment, be retested in about 3 months because reinfection is common, and be offered testing for HIV and syphilis, contraception counseling, and expedited partner therapy where permitted.

Encouraging her to involve a trusted adult, and explaining that an insurance explanation of benefits could reveal the visit, are both part of good confidential care, but neither is a condition of treatment.

why_wrong.A: Parental consent is not required for STI care, and contacting her parents against her wishes breaches confidentiality and may put her at risk of losing her home.
why_wrong.B: Referral only delays treatment and would not change the consent rules.
why_wrong.C: Chlamydia is reportable to the public health department, not to child protective services. A consensual relationship between two adolescents close in age, with no signs of abuse or coercion, is not a child protection matter in itself.
why_wrong.D: Making treatment contingent on disclosure coerces the patient and leaves an infection untreated.

objective: Minors can consent to confidential STI testing and treatment in every US state. Treat chlamydia with doxycycline for 7 days, report to public health (not parents), and retest in 3 months.
sources: Workowski KA, et al. Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021. MMWR Recomm Rep. 2021;70(4):1–187.
Guttmacher Institute. An Overview of Consent to Reproductive Health Services by Young People (state policy summary).

Society for Adolescent Health and Medicine and American Academy of Pediatrics. Confidentiality Protections for Adolescents and Young Adults in the Health Care Billing and Insurance Claims Process. J Adolesc Health. 2016;58(3):374–377.

topic: Number needed to treat from absolute risk reduction
vignette: A randomized, placebo-controlled trial enrolls 4,000 patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction who are already receiving guideline-directed therapy. Participants are assigned to a new drug (n = 2,000) or placebo (n = 2,000) for 3 years. At the end of the trial, 150 patients in the drug group and 200 patients in the placebo group have died. The investigators report a hazard ratio for death of 0.74 (95% confidence interval 0.60 to 0.91).
stem: Based on these results, approximately how many patients must be treated with the new drug for 3 years to prevent one death?
why_correct: Number needed to treat (NNT) is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction. Mortality was 200/2,000 = 10.0% with placebo and 150/2,000 = 7.5% with the drug, so the absolute risk reduction is 10.0% − 7.5% = 2.5% (0.025). NNT = 1/0.025 = 40 patients treated for 3 years to prevent one death.

The relative risk reduction is 2.5%/10% = 25%, which sounds more impressive but says nothing about how many people benefit; a 25% relative reduction of a rare outcome could mean an NNT in the thousands. Always ask for the absolute numbers. The confidence interval for the hazard ratio excludes 1.0, so the benefit is statistically significant, and the NNT applies only to the trial's time frame and a population with the same baseline risk.

why_wrong.A: 4 is 1 divided by the relative risk reduction (0.25). The reciprocal of a relative measure has no clinical meaning.
why_wrong.B: 13 is 1 divided by the drug group's mortality (0.075), which is not a risk reduction.
why_wrong.D: 100 would require an absolute risk reduction of 1 percentage point.
why_wrong.E: 400 would require an absolute risk reduction of 0.25 percentage points, a decimal-place error.

objective: NNT = 1 / absolute risk reduction, using the actual event rates in each arm, over the trial's follow-up period. Relative risk reduction cannot be used to compute it.
sources: Laupacis A, Sackett DL, Roberts RS. An assessment of clinically useful measures of the consequences of treatment. N Engl J Med. 1988;318(26):1728–1733.

topic: Lung cancer screening eligibility: 20 pack-years and quit within 15 years
vignette: A 58-year-old man comes to the office for a routine health maintenance visit. He feels well and has no cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, chest pain, or weight loss. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine and no other medical problems. He smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily from age 23 to age 45 and has not used tobacco since. He drinks two beers on weekends and does not use other substances. He works as an electrician and has had no known asbestos exposure. His father died of a myocardial infarction at age 70; there is no family history of cancer. A chest radiograph obtained 2 years ago during an episode of bronchitis was normal. Colonoscopy 4 years ago was normal.

Temperature is 36.8 C (98.2 F), blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg, pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and pulse oximetry shows 98% on room air. Body mass index is 27 kg/m<sup>2</sup>. The lungs are clear to auscultation, and there is no lymphadenopathy or clubbing. He asks whether he should have any testing for lung cancer.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Annual chest radiography
options.B: Annual low-dose CT of the chest
options.D: Low-dose CT of the chest once, with no further screening if it is normal

why_correct: Work out his exposure first. One pack per day for 22 years (age 23 to 45) is 1 × 22 = 22 pack-years, and he quit 13 years ago (age 45 to 58). The 2021 US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommendation covers adults aged 50 to 80 years with at least a 20 pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years. He meets all three conditions, so he is eligible for annual screening with low-dose CT (grade B recommendation).

The 2021 update lowered both thresholds from the 2013 version (age 55 and 30 pack-years), which roughly doubled the eligible population. The evidence comes from the National Lung Screening Trial, in which three annual low-dose CT scans reduced lung cancer mortality by about 20% compared with chest radiography in heavy smokers, and from the European NELSON trial. Screening is a shared decision: he should hear about false-positive findings (most screen-detected nodules are benign), incidental findings, radiation, and the need for yearly follow-up.

Screening stops once a person has not smoked for 15 years, or when a health problem substantially limits life expectancy or the ability or willingness to have curative lung surgery. If he stays abstinent, he would exit the program at age 60.

why_wrong.A: Chest radiography is the comparison arm that low-dose CT beat in the National Lung Screening Trial, and the PLCO trial found no mortality benefit from radiographic screening. It is not a recommended screening test.
why_wrong.C: Sputum cytology has never been shown to reduce lung cancer mortality and is not part of any screening recommendation.
why_wrong.D: A single scan misses the point of screening, which is to catch cancers as they arise. The recommendation is yearly CT for as long as the person remains eligible.
why_wrong.E: No screening would be right if he had fewer than 20 pack-years, had quit 15 or more years ago, were outside the 50 to 80 age range, or were too ill to tolerate curative treatment. None of those applies: 22 pack-years and 13 years since quitting keep him eligible for 2 more years.

objective: Offer annual low-dose CT to adults aged 50 to 80 with at least 20 pack-years who smoke or quit within the past 15 years; stop at 15 years of abstinence or when curative treatment is no longer an option. Count the pack-years and the years since quitting before deciding.
sources: US Preventive Services Task Force. Screening for Lung Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement. JAMA. 2021;325(10):962–970.
National Lung Screening Trial Research Team. Reduced lung-cancer mortality with low-dose computed tomographic screening. N Engl J Med. 2011;365(5):395–409.

topic: Postoperative delirium precipitated by an anticholinergic sleep aid
vignette: An 81-year-old woman is evaluated on the second day after open reduction and internal fixation of a right intertrochanteric hip fracture, sustained in a fall at home in which she did not strike her head. Before admission she lived alone, managed her own finances, and had no memory complaints. She has hypertension and osteoarthritis; home medications are amlodipine and acetaminophen. Since surgery she has received subcutaneous enoxaparin for prophylaxis, acetaminophen, oxycodone 5 mg as needed (two doses in the past 24 hours), and, on the first postoperative night, diphenhydramine 50 mg for difficulty sleeping.

This morning the nurse reports that the patient was calm overnight but is now pulling at her intravenous line, cannot say why she is in the hospital, and trails off in the middle of sentences. Her daughter says she was "completely herself" at a visit 12 hours earlier. Temperature is 37.1 C (98.8 F), blood pressure is 142/84 mm Hg, pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and pulse oximetry shows 96% on room air. She cannot recite the months of the year backward and her attention wanders during questions, but when her attention is held she follows commands and moves all four extremities. Pupils are equal and reactive, there is no facial asymmetry, and speech is fluent. The wound is clean and dry, and the hip pain is rated 2 of 10. Bladder ultrasonography shows 60 mL of urine; her last bowel movement was yesterday. Fingerstick glucose is 104 mg/dL. Laboratory results are shown.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: CT of the head without contrast
options.C: Physical restraints to protect the intravenous line
options.E: Stop diphenhydramine and begin reorientation, mobilization, and a sleep protocol without sedatives

why_correct: This is postoperative delirium: an acute change from her baseline, a fluctuating course (fine 12 hours ago, calm overnight, agitated now), inattention (cannot do the months backward), and disorganized thinking. Those are the four features of the Confusion Assessment Method, and inattention is the one that separates delirium from dementia. Hyperactive delirium like hers is easy to spot; the hypoactive form, which is at least as common, is often missed.

Delirium is a symptom with a cause. The vignette rules out the common ones: no hypoxia, no fever or leukocytosis, normal glucose and electrolytes, no urinary retention, no constipation, pain controlled, no head injury. What remains is a new drug. Diphenhydramine is strongly anticholinergic; the 2023 American Geriatrics Society (AGS) Beers Criteria say to avoid first-generation antihistamines in adults 65 and older because they cause confusion, and clearance falls with age. The first step is to stop it (and to avoid other deliriogenic drugs such as benzodiazepines and, where possible, to use nonopioid analgesia).

The 2015 AGS guideline on postoperative delirium recommends multicomponent nonpharmacologic care as the treatment: reorient the patient, involve family, restore glasses and hearing aids, mobilize early, keep day-night cues and a sleep routine without hypnotics, maintain hydration and nutrition, and avoid restraints and tethers such as unnecessary lines and catheters. Antipsychotics are reserved for the patient who is severely agitated and threatening substantial harm to herself or others despite those measures, at the lowest dose for the shortest time.

why_wrong.A: Head CT is indicated for delirium with focal neurologic signs, head trauma, or a fall while anticoagulated at treatment doses. She has none of these, and the picture has an obvious precipitant.
why_wrong.B: Benzodiazepines deepen and prolong delirium in older adults and are not first-line for agitation. They are the right choice only when delirium is caused by alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
why_wrong.C: Restraints increase agitation, injury, and the duration of delirium. The AGS guideline specifically advises avoiding them; a sitter or family presence protects the line better.
why_wrong.D: Antipsychotics are a last resort for severe agitation that threatens harm, given as needed at the lowest dose, never scheduled. They do not shorten delirium and add QT prolongation, extrapyramidal effects, and aspiration risk.

objective: An acute, fluctuating change in attention after surgery in an older adult is delirium: find and remove the precipitant (here an anticholinergic antihistamine), treat with multicomponent nonpharmacologic measures, avoid benzodiazepines and restraints, and keep antipsychotics for dangerous agitation only.
sources: American Geriatrics Society Expert Panel on Postoperative Delirium in Older Adults. American Geriatrics Society abstracted clinical practice guideline for postoperative delirium in older adults. J Am Geriatr Soc. 2015;63(1):142–150.

American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria Update Expert Panel. American Geriatrics Society 2023 updated AGS Beers Criteria for potentially inappropriate medication use in older adults. J Am Geriatr Soc. 2023;71(7):2052–2081.
Inouye SK, et al. Clarifying confusion: the confusion assessment method. A new method for detection of delirium. Ann Intern Med. 1990;113(12):941–948.

topic: Palpable breast mass in a woman younger than 30: ultrasonography first
vignette: A 26-year-old woman comes to the office because of a lump in her left breast that she noticed 7 weeks ago while showering. It has not changed in size and is not painful. She has had no nipple discharge, skin changes, fever, or weight loss. Menarche was at age 12, menses are regular, and her last menstrual period began 10 days ago. She takes a combined oral contraceptive and has never been pregnant. Her mother is healthy; a maternal aunt was diagnosed with breast cancer at age 62. She does not smoke and drinks alcohol occasionally.

Temperature is 36.9 C (98.4 F), blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg, pulse is 76/min, and respirations are 14/min. Examination of the left breast shows a 2-cm, firm, smooth, mobile, nontender mass in the upper outer quadrant without overlying skin change, nipple retraction, or discharge. The right breast is normal. There is no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Breast MRI
options.E: Reassurance and re-examination after the next menstrual period

why_correct: A discrete, persistent breast mass needs imaging regardless of the patient's age or lack of risk factors; the question is which test comes first, and that is decided by age. For women younger than 30, the American College of Radiology (ACR) Appropriateness Criteria (2022 update) and the ACOG practice bulletin on benign breast disorders both make ultrasonography the initial study. Young breasts are dense, which hides masses on mammography, and the pretest probability of cancer is low, so ultrasound gives more information with no radiation.

Ultrasound sorts the mass into three paths. A simple cyst needs nothing further. A solid mass with benign features (oval, circumscribed, parallel orientation), most often a fibroadenoma in this age group, can be followed with short-interval imaging or biopsied if the patient prefers or it grows. A mass with suspicious features (BI-RADS 4 or 5) goes on to diagnostic mammography and image-guided core-needle biopsy. The clinical examination, imaging, and pathology together form the triple assessment; all three should agree before a mass is called benign.

The age cutoffs are the testable fact: ultrasound first under 30; diagnostic mammography (with ultrasound) first at 40 and older; between 30 and 39 either study may begin the workup, and most practices do both.

why_wrong.A: MRI is used for high-risk screening, for assessing the extent of a known cancer, and for occult primaries. It is not an initial test for a palpable mass and generates many false positives.
why_wrong.C: Biopsy is the right next step once imaging shows a solid or suspicious mass, and imaging guides where to sample. Going straight to biopsy skips the step that would spare her a procedure if the mass is a simple cyst.
why_wrong.D: Mammography leads the workup at age 40 and older (and is reasonable from 30). In a 26-year-old it is usually not appropriate as the first test because dense tissue lowers its sensitivity.
why_wrong.E: Watchful waiting through a cycle is acceptable only for vague thickening or nodularity examined in the luteal phase. A 2-cm discrete mass that has persisted for 7 weeks has already declared itself and should be imaged now.

objective: For a palpable breast mass, image first and choose the test by age: ultrasonography under 30, diagnostic mammography plus ultrasonography at 40 and older, either between 30 and 39. Never dismiss a persistent mass because the patient is young.
sources: Klein KA, et al. ACR Appropriateness Criteria Palpable Breast Masses: 2022 Update. J Am Coll Radiol. 2023;20(5S):S146–S163.
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. Diagnosis and management of benign breast disorders. Practice Bulletin No. 164. Obstet Gynecol. 2016;127:e141–e156.

topic: Acute ischemic stroke: blood pressure above 185/110 mm Hg must be lowered before thrombolysis
vignette: A 67-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 70 minutes after the sudden onset of weakness of the right arm and difficulty speaking while eating dinner; her family witnessed the onset. She has hypertension and hyperlipidemia; medications are hydrochlorothiazide and atorvastatin. She takes no antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs and has had no recent surgery, bleeding, or head trauma. Temperature is 36.8 C (98.2 F), blood pressure is 198/112 mm Hg, pulse is 84/min and regular, respirations are 16/min, and pulse oximetry shows 97% on room air.

She is alert. There is a right facial droop, the right arm drifts with 3/5 strength, there is mild right leg weakness, and speech is nonfluent with intact comprehension; the NIH Stroke Scale score is 9. Fingerstick glucose is 118 mg/dL. Noncontrast CT of the head shows no hemorrhage and no early ischemic changes, and CT angiography shows no large-vessel occlusion. Platelet count is 232,000/µL and INR is 1.0. Fifteen minutes later, with the patient resting quietly, blood pressure is 194/110 mm Hg.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Intravenous labetalol, then intravenous thrombolysis once blood pressure is below 185/110 mm Hg
options.B: Intravenous nicardipine infusion to a systolic pressure below 140 mm Hg, then intravenous thrombolysis
options.C: Intravenous tenecteplase now, then lower the blood pressure
options.E: Oral aspirin and admission for blood pressure control without thrombolysis

why_correct: She is a thrombolysis candidate: a disabling deficit (NIHSS 9), a witnessed onset 85 minutes ago (well inside the 4.5-hour window), no hemorrhage on CT, no anticoagulant use, and normal platelets, INR, and glucose. One thing blocks treatment: blood pressure above 185/110 mm Hg. Severe hypertension at the time of thrombolysis raises the risk of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage, so it has been an exclusion since the original NINDS trial.

The 2026 American Heart Association/American Stroke Association guideline keeps the same targets: lower the pressure to below 185/110 mm Hg before intravenous thrombolysis, then hold it below 180/105 mm Hg for the first 24 hours. The guideline's agents are intravenous labetalol (10–20 mg over 1–2 minutes, repeated once if needed), a nicardipine infusion (5 mg/h, titrated by 2.5 mg/h every 5–15 minutes to a maximum of 15 mg/h), or clevidipine. These act within minutes and are titratable, so treating the pressure should not delay the drug by more than a few minutes; if the pressure cannot be brought under control, thrombolysis is withheld.

Once the pressure is below 185/110 mm Hg, give tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (maximum 25 mg) as a single bolus or alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg, 10% as a bolus and the rest over 60 minutes); the 2026 guideline endorses both. Antiplatelet therapy is held for 24 hours after thrombolysis, and blood pressure and neurologic checks continue every 15 minutes during and after the infusion.

why_wrong.B: Over-lowering is harmful: a pressure in the 180s still perfuses the ischemic penumbra, and the 2026 guideline recommends against intensive lowering (systolic below 140 mm Hg) around thrombolysis because it does not improve outcomes. The target is below 185/110, not normotension.
why_wrong.C: Thrombolysis at 194/110 mm Hg is contraindicated; the drug waits until the pressure is controlled. The sequence matters, and controlling the pressure takes minutes.
why_wrong.D: Thrombectomy is for large-vessel occlusion, and CT angiography shows none. Even when there is an occlusion, eligible patients receive thrombolysis first rather than instead.
why_wrong.E: Aspirin alone is the fallback for patients who are not thrombolysis candidates, such as those beyond the window or on anticoagulants. A blood pressure that can be lowered in minutes is not a reason to forgo reperfusion.

objective: Blood pressure above 185/110 mm Hg is the one correctable contraindication to thrombolysis: treat it with intravenous labetalol, nicardipine, or clevidipine to below 185/110, give the thrombolytic, then keep the pressure below 180/105 for 24 hours. Do not thrombolyse first and do not over-lower.
sources: Prabhakaran S, et al. 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke: A Guideline From the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association. Stroke. 2026; published online January 26, 2026.
Powers WJ, et al. Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke: 2019 Update to the 2018 Guidelines. Stroke. 2019;50(12):e344–e418.

topic: Magnesium sulfate toxicity during treatment of preeclampsia with renal impairment
vignette: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 35 weeks 4 days' gestation is admitted because of a blood pressure of 172/112 mm Hg on two measurements 20 minutes apart and a persistent headache unrelieved by acetaminophen; the pregnancy had been uncomplicated until this week. Admission laboratory results are shown. She receives intravenous labetalol, after which blood pressure is 152/96 mm Hg, and magnesium sulfate, 4 g intravenously over 20 minutes followed by an infusion of 2 g per hour. Labor is induced with oxytocin, and an epidural with bupivacaine and fentanyl is placed 2 hours later.

Five hours after the magnesium infusion was started, the nurse reports that the patient is hard to wake. Temperature is 36.9 C (98.4 F), blood pressure is 148/92 mm Hg, pulse is 88/min, respirations are 9/min, and pulse oximetry shows 93% on room air. She opens her eyes to voice and answers slowly. Patellar reflexes are absent bilaterally. Breath sounds are clear and the cervix is 4 cm dilated. Urine output over the past 4 hours has been 110 mL. The fetal heart rate tracing shows a baseline of 135/min with moderate variability and no decelerations. Serum magnesium concentration is 11.6 mg/dL.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Administer intravenous calcium gluconate and stop the magnesium infusion
options.B: Decrease the magnesium infusion to 1 g per hour
options.C: Intravenous furosemide, continuing the magnesium infusion at the current rate

why_correct: She has preeclampsia with severe features: severe-range blood pressure with a persistent headache, and a creatinine above 1.1 mg/dL. (The platelet count and transaminases are abnormal but sit below the severe-feature thresholds of 100,000/µL and twice the upper limit of normal.) Delivery and seizure prophylaxis with magnesium sulfate are therefore correct. The error was the dose. Magnesium is cleared entirely by the kidney, and ACOG Practice Bulletin 222 says that with mild renal insufficiency (creatinine 1.0–1.5 mg/dL) or oliguria (less than 30 mL/h for more than 4 hours) the 4–6 g loading dose should be followed by a maintenance infusion of only 1 g per hour, with serum magnesium levels every 4 hours. She received 2 g per hour, and her output (110 mL over 4 hours = 27.5 mL/h) was oliguric, so magnesium accumulated.

The clinical signs track the level. ACOG's table puts loss of patellar reflexes above about 9 mg/dL (7 mEq/L), respiratory paralysis above about 12 mg/dL (10 mEq/L), and cardiac arrest above about 30 mg/dL (25 mEq/L). At 11.6 mg/dL with absent reflexes and a respiratory rate of 9/min she is on the edge of respiratory arrest. Magnesium causes this by blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, which calcium directly antagonizes.

The bulletin's instruction is to stop the infusion when the level exceeds 9.6 mg/dL (8 mEq/L) and, for impending respiratory depression, to give calcium gluconate 10%, 10 mL intravenously over 3 minutes, with intravenous furosemide to speed urinary excretion and tracheal intubation if ventilation fails. Recheck the level every 2 hours; the infusion can be restarted at a lower rate once the level is below 8.4 mg/dL (7 mEq/L). Delivery proceeds once she is stable; at 35 weeks with severe features, ACOG recommends delivery after maternal stabilization, and vaginal delivery remains appropriate with a reassuring fetal tracing.

why_wrong.B: One gram per hour is the rate she should have been on from the start, but with a level of 11.6 mg/dL and respiratory depression, continuing any magnesium is dangerous. Rate reduction is for a patient with renal impairment who has not yet become toxic.
why_wrong.C: Furosemide is an adjunct that is given alongside calcium, not instead of it, and never while the infusion continues. It does nothing for the neuromuscular blockade in the next few minutes.
why_wrong.D: Epidural fentanyl is the red herring. Opioid depression would not abolish patellar reflexes, and a magnesium level of 11.6 mg/dL explains everything; naloxone would waste the minutes in which the antidote is needed.
why_wrong.E: Delivery is the cure for preeclampsia, but the fetus is reassuring and the immediate threat is maternal respiratory arrest. Operating on a hypoventilating mother before reversing the magnesium would add anesthetic risk to an untreated emergency; stabilize her first.

objective: Magnesium sulfate accumulates when the kidneys are impaired: use 1 g/h and check levels every 4 hours if creatinine is 1.0 to 1.5 mg/dL or the patient is oliguric. Loss of patellar reflexes is the first sign of toxicity; respiratory depression means stop the infusion and give calcium gluconate 10%, 10 mL IV.
sources: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. Gestational hypertension and preeclampsia. ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222. Obstet Gynecol. 2020;135(6):e237–e260.

topic: Giant cell arteritis with transient vision loss: glucocorticoids before biopsy
vignette: A 74-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 10-minute episode of painless loss of vision in the right eye 2 hours ago, "like a curtain coming down," which resolved on its own. For 3 weeks she has had a new, persistent headache over the right temple, pain in her jaw when she chews that stops when she rests, and aching stiffness of the shoulders and hips that is worst in the morning. She has lost 2 kg (4.4 lb). She has hypertension treated with lisinopril and takes no other medications. She does not smoke.

Temperature is 37.4 C (99.3 F), blood pressure is 146/84 mm Hg, pulse is 80/min and regular, and respirations are 14/min. The right superficial temporal artery is tender and thickened with a diminished pulse. Visual acuity is 20/25 in both eyes, pupils are equal and reactive without an afferent pupillary defect, and the optic discs appear normal. There are no carotid bruits. The remainder of the neurologic examination is normal. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm. Laboratory results are shown.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Aspirin 81 mg daily and ophthalmology referral within 1 week
options.D: Temporal artery biopsy before any treatment
options.E: Temporal artery ultrasonography before any treatment

why_correct: Every feature points to giant cell arteritis (GCA): age over 50, a new headache, jaw claudication (the finding that most raises the likelihood of the diagnosis, with a likelihood ratio of about 4), polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms, an abnormal temporal artery, and the laboratory signature of a markedly elevated ESR and CRP with normocytic anemia and thrombocytosis. Her transient monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax) is arteritic ischemia of the optic nerve or retina, and it is the warning that precedes permanent loss: untreated, anterior ischemic optic neuropathy can blind the eye within days and then threaten the other eye.

Vision lost to GCA rarely returns, so glucocorticoids are started the moment the diagnosis is suspected, and nothing is allowed to delay them. The 2021 American College of Rheumatology/Vasculitis Foundation guideline conditionally recommends intravenous pulse glucocorticoids rather than high-dose oral therapy for newly diagnosed GCA with threatened vision loss; the EULAR recommendations give the range as 0.25–1 g of intravenous methylprednisolone daily for up to 3 days, followed by high-dose oral prednisone. Without visual symptoms, high-dose oral prednisone (about 1 mg/kg per day, up to 60–80 mg) is the choice.

Confirmation comes afterward: the guideline recommends a unilateral temporal artery biopsy within 2 weeks of starting glucocorticoids, because the histologic changes persist for weeks on treatment, and it prefers biopsy over ultrasonography or MRI for establishing the diagnosis. Tocilizumab is added as a glucocorticoid-sparing agent, and the taper runs over a year or more with monitoring for relapse.

why_wrong.A: Aspirin is recommended only for GCA with critical or flow-limiting vertebral or carotid involvement, and a referral in a week leaves her unprotected during the days when permanent vision loss is most likely.
why_wrong.B: Twenty milligrams is a polymyalgia rheumatica dose. GCA needs high-dose therapy even without visual symptoms, and with threatened vision the guideline prefers intravenous pulses.
why_wrong.D: Biopsy is the right test but the wrong time: it should follow treatment within 2 weeks, and waiting for it risks blindness. Steroids do not meaningfully lower the biopsy yield in that window.
why_wrong.E: Ultrasonography (the halo sign) is an accepted alternative in experienced centers, but the guideline prefers biopsy, and like biopsy it must never delay glucocorticoids when vision is at risk.

objective: Suspected giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms is treated immediately with intravenous pulse glucocorticoids; without visual symptoms, high-dose oral prednisone. Temporal artery biopsy follows within 2 weeks and must never delay treatment.
