sources: Maz M, et al. 2021 American College of Rheumatology/Vasculitis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Giant Cell Arteritis and Takayasu Arteritis. Arthritis Care Res. 2021;73(8):1071–1087.
Smetana GW, Shmerling RH. Does this patient have temporal arteritis? JAMA. 2002;287(1):92–101.
Hellmich B, et al. 2018 Update of the EULAR recommendations for the management of large vessel vasculitis. Ann Rheum Dis. 2020;79(1):19–30.

topic: Blunt abdominal trauma: a transient responder with a positive FAST goes to the operating room
vignette: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 25 minutes after a motorcycle collision in which he was thrown over the handlebars. He was wearing a helmet. He is awake and complains of abdominal pain. Temperature is 36.2 C (97.2 F), blood pressure is 84/52 mm Hg, pulse is 128/min, respirations are 26/min, and pulse oximetry shows 97% on oxygen by nonrebreather mask. He is anxious, and the skin is cool and pale. The airway is patent, breath sounds are equal, and the trachea is midline. There are abrasions over the left flank and lower left chest; the abdomen is distended and diffusely tender with guarding. The pelvis is stable to compression, and there is no external hemorrhage. The Glasgow Coma Scale score is 15. Chest and pelvic radiographs show no pneumothorax, hemothorax, or fracture.

Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) shows free fluid in the hepatorenal and splenorenal spaces and in the pelvis; the pericardial view is normal. Two large-bore intravenous lines are placed, and 1 L of warmed lactated Ringer solution is infused. Blood pressure rises to 108/70 mm Hg and pulse falls to 104/min. Ten minutes later, blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg and pulse is 132/min. Hemoglobin on arrival was 11.8 g/dL, and serum lactate is 5.4 mmol/L. Type O-negative blood is available, and the trauma surgeon is at the bedside.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Angiographic embolization
options.B: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast
options.D: Exploratory laparotomy with activation of the massive transfusion protocol
options.E: Second 1-L bolus of lactated Ringer solution and repeat FAST

why_correct: He arrived in hemorrhagic shock (hypotension, a pulse above 120, tachypnea, cool skin: ATLS class III or worse, meaning more than 30% of blood volume lost) after blunt trauma with no external bleeding, no hemothorax, and a stable pelvis. The FAST shows free fluid in three windows, so the blood is in the abdomen; the left flank and lower rib abrasions make the spleen the likely source. The normal arrival hemoglobin is a red herring: it has not had time to equilibrate, while the lactate of 5.4 mmol/L shows real hypoperfusion.

The response to fluid is the decisive clue. ATLS classifies patients as rapid responders, transient responders, or nonresponders to an initial bolus. He is a transient responder: pressure improved, then collapsed again within minutes. That pattern means bleeding is continuing faster than it can be replaced, and the only treatment is to stop the bleeding. A hemodynamically unstable patient with a positive FAST needs an exploratory laparotomy; the Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma guideline on blunt abdominal trauma states this directly, and nothing in the vignette argues for delay.

Resuscitation on the way to the operating room is with blood, not more crystalloid. ATLS (10th edition) limits the initial crystalloid bolus to about 1 L in adults and moves transient and nonresponders straight to blood products, given in a balanced ratio of plasma, platelets, and red cells (the PROPPR trial's 1:1:1). The 11th edition (2025) goes further in the same direction, with hemorrhage control placed first in the primary survey and damage-control resuscitation that limits crystalloid. Large volumes of crystalloid dilute clotting factors, cool the patient, and feed the triad of acidosis, hypothermia, and coagulopathy.

why_wrong.A: Embolization is for solid-organ bleeding in a stable patient, usually a contrast blush on CT, and in some centers for a transient responder whose injury has already been defined. It requires a CT and a patient who can tolerate the angiography suite; he has neither.
why_wrong.B: CT is the test for the hemodynamically stable patient with a positive FAST. An unstable patient in the scanner can arrest with no one able to intervene.
why_wrong.C: Peritoneal lavage answers the question the FAST has already answered (is there blood in the belly?) and would only delay the operation. Its remaining role is the unstable patient in whom FAST is unavailable or equivocal.
why_wrong.E: A second liter treats the number, not the bleeding, and the first bolus already failed. ATLS stops at about 1 L before switching to blood, because further crystalloid worsens coagulopathy and raises mortality.

objective: A transient response to the initial fluid bolus means ongoing hemorrhage. With a positive FAST and hemodynamic instability, the next step is laparotomy with blood-product resuscitation, not CT, not more crystalloid.
sources: American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma. Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) Student Course Manual. 10th ed. Chicago, IL: American College of Surgeons; 2018.
Hoff WS, et al. Practice management guidelines for the evaluation of blunt abdominal trauma: the EAST Practice Management Guidelines Work Group. J Trauma. 2002;53(3):602–615.

Holcomb JB, et al. Transfusion of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells in a 1:1:1 vs a 1:1:2 ratio and mortality in patients with severe trauma: the PROPPR randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2015;313(5):471–482.
American College of Surgeons. Trauma care gets major upgrade with launch of ATLS 11. ACS Brief. September 16, 2025.

topic: Chronic lithium toxicity precipitated by an ACE inhibitor: when to dialyze
vignette: A 54-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband because of 3 days of worsening confusion, unsteady walking, and vomiting. She has bipolar I disorder that has been stable for 12 years on lithium carbonate 900 mg daily; her lithium level 4 months ago was 0.8 mEq/L. She also has hypertension, for which her primary care physician started lisinopril 4 weeks ago, and type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin. She has not taken extra lithium, and her husband confirms the pill count. For a week she has had a poor appetite and been drinking little.

Temperature is 37.3 C (99.1 F), blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, pulse is 96/min, respirations are 16/min, and pulse oximetry shows 97% on room air. Mucous membranes are dry. She is drowsy but arousable and oriented to person only. There is a coarse tremor of both hands, dysarthria, diffuse hyperreflexia with sustained ankle clonus, and a wide-based, unsteady gait. ECG shows sinus rhythm at 96/min without conduction abnormality. Laboratory results are shown. Intravenous isotonic saline is started.
stem: In addition to stopping lithium and lisinopril, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Continued intravenous isotonic saline with lithium levels every 4 hours

why_correct: This is chronic lithium toxicity: a stable dose that became toxic because clearance fell. Lithium is handled by the kidney like sodium, and two things cut its clearance here. The lisinopril started 4 weeks ago is the first; the lithium prescribing information lists renin-angiotensin system antagonists (lisinopril, enalapril, captopril, valsartan) as drugs that raise steady-state lithium concentrations and calls for closer monitoring and dose reduction when they are added. The second is volume depletion from a week of poor intake, which both reduces glomerular filtration and increases proximal tubular reabsorption of sodium and lithium. The result is a creatinine of 2.3 mg/dL and a level of 4.4 mEq/L. Chronic toxicity produces neurologic signs (tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, hyperreflexia, clonus, confusion) at lower levels than an acute overdose, because the brain has had time to load.

The EXTRIP workgroup's 2015 recommendations define when lithium should be removed by dialysis. Extracorporeal treatment is recommended when kidney function is impaired and the level is above 4.0 mEq/L, or when there is a decreased level of consciousness, seizures, or a life-threatening dysrhythmia regardless of the level; it is suggested when the level is above 5.0 mEq/L, when there is significant confusion, or when the expected time to bring the level below 1.0 mEq/L with optimal care exceeds 36 hours. She meets two of the recommended criteria (impaired kidney function with a level of 4.4, and decreased consciousness) and one of the suggested ones.

Lithium is an ideal dialysis target: a small ion with no protein binding and a modest volume of distribution. Intermittent hemodialysis is the preferred modality; continuous therapy is an acceptable alternative when intermittent dialysis is unavailable. Treatment continues until the level is below 1.0 mEq/L or there is clear clinical improvement (or for at least 6 hours if levels are not readily available), followed by serial levels over the next 12 hours because lithium redistributes from tissue and rebounds. Saline continues alongside to restore glomerular filtration, with attention to the sodium of 146 mEq/L, which hints at lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

why_wrong.A: Saline alone is the treatment for mild toxicity with intact kidney function and no neurologic signs. With impaired kidneys, a level above 4.0, and encephalopathy, waiting on saline leaves the brain exposed for a day or more.
why_wrong.B: Lithium does not bind to activated charcoal. Charcoal has a role only for co-ingestants.
why_wrong.C: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate binds lithium weakly in vitro and is not recommended; it would also drive the potassium down.
why_wrong.E: Whole-bowel irrigation is for a large, recent ingestion of sustained-release lithium with pills still in the gut. There was no ingestion here; the drug is already in her tissues.

objective: Lithium toxicity in a patient on a stable dose means clearance fell: look for a new ACE inhibitor, ARB, diuretic, or NSAID and for volume depletion. Dialyze when kidney function is impaired and the level exceeds 4.0 mEq/L, or whenever consciousness is depressed, seizures occur, or a dangerous dysrhythmia appears.
sources: Decker BS, Goldfarb DS, Dargan PI, et al. Extracorporeal treatment for lithium poisoning: systematic review and recommendations from the EXTRIP Workgroup. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2015;10(5):875–887.
Lithium carbonate capsules and tablets: prescribing information (section 7.1, Drug Interactions). US Food and Drug Administration; revised December 2018.

topic: Fever in a well-appearing 14-day-old: lumbar puncture, parenteral antibiotics, and admission regardless of normal urinalysis and markers
vignette: A 14-day-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of a rectal temperature of 38.3 C (100.9 F) measured at home 2 hours ago. He has been fussier than usual since the morning but breastfeeds every 2 to 3 hours and had six wet diapers yesterday. He has had no vomiting, cough, or rash. He was born at 39 weeks' gestation by uncomplicated vaginal delivery; his mother's group B streptococcal screen was negative, she had no fever during labor, and she has no history of genital herpes. He went home on the second day of life and received intramuscular vitamin K at birth. His 3-year-old sister has had a runny nose for 4 days.

He weighs 3.8 kg (8 lb 6 oz); birth weight was 3.4 kg (7 lb 8 oz). Temperature is 38.4 C (101.1 F) rectally, pulse is 158/min, respirations are 44/min, and pulse oximetry shows 98% on room air. He is alert, cries vigorously during the examination, and is consoled when held. The anterior fontanelle is soft and flat, and there is mild clear rhinorrhea. The tympanic membranes, lungs, heart, abdomen, umbilicus, and skin are normal, with no vesicles. Capillary refill time is less than 2 seconds. A urine specimen is obtained by catheterization, and blood is drawn for culture. Laboratory results are shown.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Discharge home with reassessment in 24 hours

why_correct: Three facts decide this case: the infant is 14 days old, the rectal temperature is 38.4 C (fever is 38.0 C or higher), and he looks well. The 2021 American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) clinical practice guideline on well-appearing febrile infants 8 to 60 days old sorts infants into three age strata (8 to 21, 22 to 28, and 29 to 60 days) because the risk of invasive bacterial infection falls week by week: in the PECARN cohort, bacteremia was found in 5.3% of febrile infants in the second week of life and 3.3% in the third, against 1.6% in the fourth, and bacterial meningitis occurs in 0.5% to 1.3% of febrile infants 8 to 21 days old. No examination finding and no laboratory marker lowers that risk enough to skip any part of the evaluation at this age.

For infants 8 to 21 days the key action statements (KAS) are all firm: obtain urine by catheterization or suprapubic aspiration for urinalysis, with culture if the urinalysis is positive (KAS 1; evidence grade A, strong recommendation); obtain a blood culture (KAS 2; A, strong); obtain cerebrospinal fluid for cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, and culture (KAS 4; A, strong); start parenteral antimicrobial therapy (KAS 5; A, strong); and monitor the infant in a hospital with staff experienced in the care of young infants (KAS 6; B, moderate). Inflammatory markers are optional at this age (KAS 3; B, weak): his normal absolute neutrophil count (3,400/µL; the guideline's cutoff is 4,000/µL when procalcitonin is also measured and 5,200/µL when it is not) and C-reactive protein (0.6 mg/dL, that is 6 mg/L, against a cutoff of 20 mg/L) change none of these steps, though they may help later in deciding when to stop antibiotics. The lumbar puncture comes before the antibiotics: cerebrospinal fluid drawn after a dose is hard to interpret, and an infant with uncertain meningitis ends up with a prolonged course.

The runny-nosed sister and the infant's mild rhinorrhea are a red herring. Upper respiratory symptoms do not take an infant out of the pathway, and infants younger than 28 days with a positive viral test still carry a 1.1% to 2.1% risk of invasive bacterial infection, which the guideline judges high enough to warrant the same testing and treatment. The history also matters for herpes simplex virus: there is no maternal genital herpes, and he has no vesicles, seizures, or hypothermia, so empiric acyclovir is not indicated unless the cerebrospinal fluid shows pleocytosis with a negative Gram stain or there is leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, or an elevated alanine aminotransferase.

Empiric therapy at 8 to 21 days with no focus identified (guideline Table 3) is ampicillin 150 mg/kg per day intravenously divided every 8 hours plus either ceftazidime 150 mg/kg per day divided every 8 hours or gentamicin 4 mg/kg every 24 hours. For 3.8 kg: ampicillin 3.8 × 50 = 190 mg every 8 hours, with ceftazidime 190 mg every 8 hours or gentamicin 3.8 × 4 = 15 mg every 24 hours. Ampicillin covers Listeria and enterococci; Escherichia coli is now the most common cause of bacteremia and group B streptococcus the most common cause of meningitis in this age group. If all cultures are negative at 24 to 36 hours and he remains well, antibiotics are stopped and he goes home (KAS 7a; B, strong).

why_wrong.A: Home management belongs to the 29- to 60-day pathway: a well-appearing infant of that age with a negative urinalysis and normal inflammatory markers may be observed at home without antibiotics and reassessed in 24 hours (KAS 20d). At 14 days the guideline makes no such allowance, whatever the laboratory results show.
why_wrong.B: Observation in hospital without antibiotics is an option for a 29- to 60-day-old whose urinalysis is negative, whose markers are normal, and whose cerebrospinal fluid, if obtained, is normal (KAS 19d). At 8 to 21 days parenteral antibiotics are a strong recommendation (KAS 5); withholding them while cultures incubate leaves a roughly 1-in-20 chance of bacteremia untreated.
why_wrong.C: A dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone with discharge is the older outpatient strategy for infants 29 days and older, and the guideline still allows a parenteral antibiotic with observation at home for a 29- to 60-day-old whose markers are abnormal but whose cerebrospinal fluid is normal (Figure 3). A 14-day-old is admitted, the antibiotic follows the lumbar puncture, and ceftriaxone is not in the guideline's regimens for 8 to 21 days: it displaces bilirubin from albumin, must not be given to hyperbilirubinemic neonates, and is contraindicated in neonates 28 days or younger who need calcium-containing intravenous solutions.
why_wrong.E: Procalcitonin is the most accurate inflammatory marker, and at 22 to 60 days the markers should be assessed (KAS 10 and 17) because an abnormal value changes what follows: cerebrospinal fluid should be obtained at 22 to 28 days (KAS 11b) and may be at 29 to 60 days (KAS 18a), and parenteral antibiotics may be given (KAS 12b and 19b). At 8 to 21 days they are optional (KAS 3) because every infant is tested, treated, and admitted regardless; waiting for a procalcitonin result would only delay the lumbar puncture.

objective: A well-appearing term infant 8 to 21 days old with a rectal temperature of 38.0 C or higher needs urinalysis by catheter, blood culture, and lumbar puncture, then parenteral antibiotics and hospital monitoring, whatever the urinalysis, inflammatory markers, or viral symptoms show. Marker-guided decisions and home management begin at 22 days.
sources: Pantell RH, Roberts KB, Adams WG, et al; Subcommittee on Febrile Infants. Clinical Practice Guideline: Evaluation and Management of Well-Appearing Febrile Infants 8 to 60 Days Old. Pediatrics. 2021;148(2):e2021052228 (Key Action Statements 1–7, Figure 1, Table 3; revised version posted October 28, 2021, per the Statement of Correction, Pediatrics 2021;148(5):e2021054063).

Mace SE, Gemme SR, Valente JH, et al. Clinical Policy for Well-Appearing Infants and Children Younger Than 2 Years of Age Presenting to the Emergency Department With Fever. Ann Emerg Med. 2016;67(5):625–639 (excludes neonates 28 days and younger).

topic: Suspected intussusception in an 8-month-old: ultrasonography before enema reduction
vignette: An 8-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her father because of episodes of crying that began 7 hours ago. Every 15 to 20 minutes she screams, pulls her knees to her chest, and cannot be comforted for several minutes; between episodes she lies quietly and is sleepy. She has vomited twice; the vomitus was formula without bile. She has had no fever or diarrhea. A runny nose and loose stools last week have resolved. She was born at term, takes formula and pureed foods, and her immunizations are up to date.

She weighs 8.0 kg (17 lb 10 oz). Temperature is 37.6 C (99.7 F), pulse is 148/min, respirations are 36/min, and blood pressure is 92/58 mm Hg. She is drowsy but opens her eyes and cries when her abdomen is palpated. The anterior fontanelle is soft and flat. Mucous membranes are moist, the extremities are warm, and capillary refill time is 2 seconds. The abdomen is soft and not distended, with an ill-defined, tubular, mildly tender mass in the right upper quadrant; the right lower quadrant feels empty. There is no guarding or rebound tenderness. The diaper contains a small amount of loose stool mixed with mucus that tests positive for occult blood. There are no inguinal hernias.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Abdominal radiography
options.D: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast

why_correct: Put the findings together. Paroxysms of colicky pain every 15 to 20 minutes in which the infant draws up her legs, quiet or sleepy intervals between them, nonbilious vomiting, a tubular mass in the right upper quadrant with an empty right lower quadrant, and stool with mucus and occult blood describe ileocolic intussusception, in which the terminal ileum telescopes through the ileocecal valve into the colon. It is a disease of infants and toddlers (most cases occur between 3 and 36 months, and about 83% before age 3), usually with no lead point at this age and often after a viral illness. The classic combination of pain, vomiting, bloody stool, and a palpable mass is present in only about 20% of children, and lethargy or irritability is common in the youngest patients.

The diagnosis is confirmed before it is treated, and the test is abdominal ultrasonography. The American College of Radiology (ACR) Appropriateness Criteria for abdominal pain in a child (new 2025, published 2026) rate ultrasonography 'usually appropriate' as the initial imaging for suspected intussusception, radiography 'may be appropriate', and contrast enema, CT, and MRI 'usually not appropriate'. Ultrasonography has a sensitivity of about 98% and a specificity of 98% to 100%, needs no radiation or sedation, and shows a concentric, target-like mass in cross-section with a kidney-like appearance along its length; it also looks for a pathologic lead point, fluid trapped between the bowel layers, and absent blood flow on Doppler, findings that predict a difficult reduction. The ACR–SPR practice parameter for pediatric contrast enemas (revised 2026) states that sonography is important in establishing the diagnosis before a reduction procedure is begun.

Once ultrasonography confirms the intussusception, this child is a candidate for nonoperative reduction: she is warm and well perfused with a normal blood pressure, and her abdomen is soft without guarding, so none of the contraindications (free intraperitoneal air, peritonitis, shock) is present. Reduction is done by air or liquid enema under fluoroscopy, or by saline enema under ultrasonography, with a surgeon notified and available, intravenous access, and fluids first if she is dehydrated; the parameter advises reduction within 8 to 12 hours of the ultrasound diagnosis, a target air pressure of 120 mm Hg, and up to three attempts of up to 5 minutes each. Air enema succeeds in about 80% of cases with perforation in fewer than 1%, and a partly reduced intussusception can be tried again after a delay. The American Pediatric Surgical Association's 2021 systematic review supports observing a stable child for about 4 hours after reduction and then discharging from the emergency department, and finds no benefit from prophylactic antibiotics before reduction (the ACR–SPR parameter leaves them to the clinical service). Surgery, preferably laparoscopic, is for failed reduction, perforation, peritonitis, shock, or a lead point.

why_wrong.A: Plain radiographs are insensitive (roughly 40% to 60% in published series) and cannot confirm the diagnosis, so the ACR rates them 'may be appropriate'. Their role is to look for free air or a high-grade obstruction when perforation is a concern before an enema; once ultrasonography has made the diagnosis, radiographs add radiation without changing management. They would come first in an infant with a rigid, distended abdomen.
why_wrong.C: The air enema is the treatment, not the test. As initial imaging it is 'usually not appropriate': it exposes the child to fluoroscopy and a small risk of perforation, requires a surgeon on standby, and is unnecessary in the many infants whose colicky crying has another cause. It is the right next step after ultrasonography shows the intussusception in a stable child without peritonitis or free air.
why_wrong.D: CT is 'usually not appropriate' for suspected intussusception in a child: it delivers radiation, often needs sedation, delays treatment, and answers nothing that ultrasonography does not. Its uses in a child's abdomen lie elsewhere, for example after major blunt trauma.
why_wrong.E: Lethargy in an infant rightly raises the question of meningitis or sepsis, but here it is episodic and explained: she is afebrile, rouses and cries when examined, has a flat fontanelle, and has an abdominal mass with occult blood in the stool. A lumbar puncture would be right for a febrile, irritable infant with a bulging fontanelle, or for lethargy with no abdominal explanation; here it would delay the diagnosis while the trapped bowel becomes more ischemic.

objective: Episodic colicky pain with drawing up of the legs, lethargy between episodes, vomiting, and a right-sided abdominal mass or blood in the stool in an infant is intussusception until proven otherwise. Confirm it with abdominal ultrasonography first; reduce it by air or liquid enema only after confirmation, and only if there is no peritonitis, free air, or shock.

topic: Convulsive status epilepticus continuing after two adequate benzodiazepine doses: a second-line agent, not a third benzodiazepine
vignette: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by ambulance because of a generalized seizure that began 20 minutes ago. Her father says she has had a runny nose and fever since yesterday; she was playing when her eyes rolled upward and all four limbs began to jerk, and she has not responded since. Paramedics gave 5 mg of midazolam intramuscularly 10 minutes ago; the jerking slowed for about a minute and then resumed. At 18 months of age she had a 3-minute seizure with a fever and recovered fully. She was born at term, has no other medical history, takes no medications, and her immunizations are up to date.

She weighs 14.0 kg (30 lb 14 oz). Temperature is 39.4 C (102.9 F) rectally, pulse is 134/min, respirations are 28/min and irregular, blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg, and pulse oximetry shows 95% while she receives oxygen by face mask. Rhythmic clonic movements of all four limbs continue, and both eyes are deviated to the right. The pupils are 4 mm and reactive. The neck is supple. There is clear nasal discharge; the tympanic membranes, lungs, and skin are normal, with no rash or bruises. Point-of-care glucose is 96 mg/dL. An intravenous line is placed, blood is drawn, and lorazepam 1.4 mg (0.1 mg/kg) is given intravenously.
after_labs: Six minutes later, 26 minutes after the seizure began, the clonic movements are unchanged. She is breathing spontaneously with a jaw thrust, and pulse oximetry shows 94%.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Endotracheal intubation and propofol infusion

why_correct: This child is in convulsive status epilepticus: a generalized convulsive seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, here 26 minutes and counting, most likely febrile status epilepticus given the fever, the viral prodrome, the earlier febrile seizure, the supple neck, and the normal glucose. The American Epilepsy Society (AES) 2016 guideline organizes treatment by time from seizure onset: a stabilization phase (0 to 5 minutes: airway, oxygen, monitoring, glucose, intravenous access), an initial-therapy phase (5 to 20 minutes) in which a benzodiazepine is the treatment of choice (level A), a second-therapy phase (20 to 40 minutes), and a third-therapy phase (40 to 60 minutes). She has received two adequate benzodiazepine doses and the seizure has passed the 20-minute mark, so the next drug is a second-line agent: intravenous levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4,500 mg), fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg (maximum 1,500 mg PE), or valproate 40 mg/kg (maximum 3,000 mg), given as a single full dose.

Both doses she received were full doses. The midazolam dose follows the RAMPART protocol (5 mg intramuscularly for children weighing 13 to 40 kg; here 5 / 14.0 = 0.36 mg/kg), and the lorazepam dose is 0.1 mg/kg (14.0 × 0.1 = 1.4 mg; maximum 4 mg per dose). Both reach the minimum adequate doses that defined benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus in the ESETT trial for children under 32 kg (midazolam 0.3 mg/kg intramuscularly, that is 4.2 mg for her, or lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg intravenously). The AES guideline allows intravenous lorazepam or diazepam to be repeated once at full dose and says that initial therapies should not otherwise be given twice; after two doses, more benzodiazepine adds respiratory depression without adding seizure control. In the North London population-based study of childhood convulsive status epilepticus, treatment with more than two benzodiazepine doses was associated with respiratory depression (odds ratio 2.9) and with episodes lasting more than 60 minutes (odds ratio 3.6).

ESETT (the Established Status Epilepticus Treatment Trial, 2019) randomized 384 children and adults whose convulsive status epilepticus continued after adequate benzodiazepine to levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate: seizures stopped with improving responsiveness at 60 minutes in 47%, 45%, and 46%, with no significant difference in life-threatening hypotension, intubation, or death in the trial overall; among the 225 children (the trial's group under 18 years) the rates were 52%, 49%, and 52%, and the one safety difference in children was more intubation within 60 minutes with fosphenytoin (33%, against 8% with levetiracetam and 11% with valproate). The AES guideline, which predates ESETT, already treated the three as equivalent choices with no evidence that one is better (level U for fosphenytoin and levetiracetam, level B for valproate), so any one is acceptable, and levetiracetam is the one offered here. For 14.0 kg: levetiracetam 60 × 14.0 = 840 mg intravenously, infused over 10 minutes as in ESETT; the alternatives would be fosphenytoin 20 × 14.0 = 280 mg PE or valproate 40 × 14.0 = 560 mg. Care continues in parallel: airway positioning and oxygen, cardiorespiratory monitoring, a search for the cause (electrolytes now; because of the fever, consideration of meningitis or encephalitis once the seizure stops, with lumbar puncture and empiric antimicrobials if the examination afterward is not reassuring), and preparation for the third phase (a repeat second-line agent or an anesthetic infusion with continuous EEG monitoring in an intensive care unit) if she is still seizing at 40 minutes.

why_wrong.A: Anesthetic infusions (propofol, midazolam, pentobarbital, or thiopental) with continuous EEG monitoring belong to the third-therapy phase, for seizures that continue after an adequate second-line agent (refractory status epilepticus, from about 40 minutes), or whenever the airway or breathing fails. She is breathing spontaneously with an oxygen saturation of 94% to 95%, and the second-line drug has not yet been tried; intubation and propofol now expose her to hypotension and a prolonged intensive care stay before the drug that stops the seizure in about half of such children has been given.
why_wrong.C: A third benzodiazepine dose is the tempting error. The AES guideline permits one repeat of intravenous lorazepam or diazepam at full dose, and she has already had two adequate benzodiazepine doses (the midazolam counts); the initial-therapy phase ends at 20 minutes. Beyond two doses, benzodiazepines add respiratory depression (odds ratio 2.9 in the North London study) and are associated with seizures that last more than 60 minutes. A second lorazepam dose would be right if only one adequate dose had been given and the seizure were still in its first 20 minutes.
why_wrong.D: Phenobarbital (15 mg/kg intravenously, here 15 × 14.0 = 210 mg) is the AES alternative in both phases when the preferred drugs are not available: as initial therapy if no benzodiazepine can be given (level A) and as second therapy if fosphenytoin, valproate, and levetiracetam are all unavailable (level B). It causes more sedation and respiratory depression, which would compound two benzodiazepine doses, and the three preferred agents work in about half of children.
why_wrong.E: Rectal diazepam (0.2 to 0.5 mg/kg, maximum 20 mg) is a level B initial-therapy alternative for a patient without intravenous access, typically given at home or before hospital arrival. It is another benzodiazepine, she has an intravenous line, and she has already received two adequate doses; it would add respiratory depression and delay the second-line agent.

objective: In convulsive status epilepticus a benzodiazepine is first-line and may be repeated once; when the seizure continues after two adequate doses and 20 minutes, give a single full dose of a second-line agent (levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, or valproate 40 mg/kg, about equally effective in ESETT) rather than a third benzodiazepine, which adds respiratory depression without seizure control.

topic: Stage 1 office blood pressures on three visits in a 13-year-old: confirm with ambulatory blood pressure monitoring before the diagnosis is acted on
vignette: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother for a scheduled blood pressure recheck. At his well-child examination 4 months ago his blood pressure was 134/84 mm Hg; at a return visit 2 weeks after that it was 136/86 mm Hg in the right arm, 134/84 mm Hg in the left arm, and 148/82 mm Hg in the right leg. Each reading was obtained by auscultation with an appropriately sized cuff after 5 minutes of seated rest. He has had no headaches, visual changes, chest pain, palpitations, snoring, muscle cramps, or flushing. He takes no medications, supplements, energy drinks, or other substances, was born at term, and has never been hospitalized. His father was diagnosed with hypertension at 42 years of age; there is no family history of kidney disease or early cardiovascular death. Since the first visit he has stopped drinking soda and plays basketball three afternoons a week. Urinalysis and serum electrolyte, creatinine, and lipid values obtained at the second visit were normal.

He is at the 58th percentile for height and the 87th percentile for weight; BMI is 23.2 kg/m<sup>2</sup> (91st percentile). Blood pressure today, by auscultation in the right arm after 5 minutes of rest, is 132/86 mm Hg, and a repeat measurement 5 minutes later is 134/84 mm Hg; pulse is 72/min. Fundoscopic examination and the thyroid gland are normal. Heart sounds are normal without murmurs, and femoral pulses are strong and symmetric. There is no abdominal bruit, acanthosis nigricans, striae, or edema. Sexual maturity rating is Tanner stage 3.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
options.E: Repeat blood pressure measurement in 6 months

why_correct: For adolescents 13 years and older the 2017 American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) clinical practice guideline uses the adult thresholds (Table 3): normal below 120/80 mm Hg, elevated blood pressure 120 to 129 with a diastolic pressure below 80, stage 1 hypertension 130/80 to 139/89, and stage 2 at 140/90 or higher. Every one of his auscultatory readings over three visits (134/84; 136/86 and 134/84; 132/86 and 134/84 today) sits in the stage 1 range. The guideline's diagnostic rule is that hypertension is diagnosed from auscultatory-confirmed readings at or above the threshold on 3 different visits (Key Action Statement [KAS] 3; grade C, moderate), and its stage 1 pathway is: lifestyle counseling and a recheck in 1 to 2 weeks; if still stage 1, arm and leg pressures and a recheck in 3 months; and if still stage 1 at the third visit, ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM), the diagnostic evaluation, and treatment (section 4.3c).

The step this third visit calls for is therefore ABPM: 'ABPM should be performed for the confirmation of hypertension in children and adolescents with office blood pressure measurements in the elevated blood pressure category for 1 year or more or with stage 1 hypertension over 3 clinic visits' (KAS 6; grade C, moderate recommendation), and the management table adds that ABPM is done to confirm hypertension before the diagnostic evaluation is begun (Table 11). A 24-hour recording with a validated monitor separates sustained hypertension from white coat hypertension, which the guideline estimates in up to half of children evaluated for elevated office readings and which otherwise leads to needless testing and medication, and it detects masked and nocturnal hypertension. The 2022 American Heart Association scientific statement on pediatric ABPM makes the same point, suggesting that ABPM be used to confirm the diagnosis before antihypertensive medication is started, and it classifies an adolescent's recording as hypertensive when the 24-hour mean is 125/75 mm Hg or higher, the wake mean 130/80 or higher, or the sleep mean 110/65 or higher.

Nothing here demands a different first move. His leg pressure exceeds his arm pressures, so there is no coarctation gradient; the femoral pulses are normal; there is no bruit, no hypokalemia, no abnormal urinalysis or creatinine, and no sign of thyroid, adrenal, or other endocrine disease. He is overweight with a hypertensive father: for a child 6 years or older with a positive family history, overweight or obesity, and no history or examination finding suggesting a secondary cause, an extensive evaluation for secondary hypertension is not required (KAS 11; grade C, moderate). The screening tests for all patients (urinalysis, chemistry panel, lipid profile; Table 10) have been done. If ABPM confirms hypertension, management continues with lifestyle change (weight management, diet, and activity), and echocardiography and a drug follow only when pharmacologic treatment is being considered.

why_wrong.B: Echocardiography is recommended to assess for cardiac target-organ damage (left ventricular mass, geometry, and function) at the time pharmacologic treatment of hypertension is being considered (KAS 15; grade C, moderate), and electrocardiography is not to be used for that purpose (KAS 14). The diagnosis is unconfirmed and no drug is planned, so it is premature; it is the right step once ABPM confirms hypertension and medication is contemplated.
why_wrong.C: Pharmacologic treatment (an ACE inhibitor, angiotensin receptor blocker, long-acting calcium channel blocker, or thiazide diuretic) is for children and adolescents with hypertension who have failed lifestyle modification, particularly those with left ventricular hypertrophy, symptoms, or stage 2 hypertension without a clearly modifiable factor (KAS 21; grade B, moderate). He has asymptomatic stage 1 readings, has changed his diet and activity for only 4 months, and does not yet have a confirmed diagnosis; lisinopril now risks years of treatment for white coat hypertension.
why_wrong.D: Renal ultrasonography is a screening test for children younger than 6 years and for those with an abnormal urinalysis or renal function (Table 10), and Doppler renal ultrasonography may screen for renal artery stenosis in normal-weight children 8 years and older in whom renovascular hypertension is suspected (KAS 16; grade C): stage 2 or marked diastolic hypertension, hypokalemia, discrepant kidney sizes, or an abdominal bruit. He has none of these, he is overweight (Doppler studies perform poorly in overweight children, which is why KAS 16 is limited to normal weight), and his urinalysis and creatinine are normal.
why_wrong.E: A recheck in 6 months is the pathway for elevated blood pressure (120 to 129 with a diastolic pressure below 80 at his age): lifestyle advice and a repeat measurement in 6 months, with ABPM only if readings remain elevated after 12 months (section 4.3b). His readings are stage 1 hypertension on three visits over 4 months, which the guideline says to confirm now; another 6 months leaves possible sustained hypertension unconfirmed and untreated.

objective: In a child 6 years or older, stage 1 office hypertension (130/80 to 139/89 mm Hg from age 13) on three visits is confirmed with ambulatory blood pressure monitoring before the diagnosis is acted on; echocardiography comes when drug therapy is being considered, drugs after lifestyle change fails (or for stage 2, symptoms, or left ventricular hypertrophy), and renal imaging only for children under 6, an abnormal urinalysis or renal function, or signs of renovascular disease.
